system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.
runtime: Anthropic API, effort medium, no seed or temperature, so runs do not repeat exactly

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a new consumer product line yet. Run the proposed pedigree-versus-channel price test (about 14,000 EUR, 8 weeks, estimated) before choosing between a pedigree-led home machine and a channel partnership. Pedigree-led home sales are the more plausible starting point because Simonelli already sells a home-oriented machine, the Oscar Mood, built on commercial components, though I found no evidence on its sales or margins.

frame.objective: Decide whether Simonelli Group should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific home or prosumer use case, beyond its professional espresso-equipment offering, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; the company has not asked this question and nothing here reflects its intentions
Financial data may be incomplete; state what could not be found
Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
No SIMULATED results may be cited as evidence
alternatives: No expansion: remain professional-only, focused on commercial cafe and foodservice buyers
Product redesign: adapt existing Nuova Simonelli or Victoria Arduino machines for home or prosumer use (smaller, simpler, lower price)
Different route to buyers: sell existing prosumer machines through retailers, e-commerce or distributors, with no new product line
Different customer group: a distinct home or small-office branded line
Licensing or white-label partnership with a consumer appliance maker, keeping Simonelli's brand in professional
Adjacent accessory play: grinders or maintenance products sold to existing home-machine owners, without a full machine

T1.claim: Prosumers pay a premium for commercial-grade components and brand credibility, so a Simonelli home line sold on that heritage (e.g., the Oscar Mood's commercial-derived parts) could earn premium prices without a new product category.
T1.who_benefits: Enthusiast home buyers who want commercial-level performance and are willing to pay more for it; Simonelli, which already has the components and brand.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers treat a professional pedigree as proof of quality and durability, so they shift spend from mass-market appliances to a machine with a commercial heritage.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Price premium over mass-market home machines, sold through the existing Nuova Simonelli or Victoria Arduino brands, with margin protected by reusing commercial components.
assumptions: Prosumer buyers will pay a meaningful premium for commercial heritage over mass-market home brands
Existing components can be reused at home-machine scale without redesign costs eroding margin
Simonelli's brand carries credibility outside the cafe trade
predictions: Prosumer buyers in a survey or store test rate commercial pedigree as a top purchase reason
Price elasticity is low enough that a 20-40% premium over comparable home machines holds conversion
Sales concentrate among existing cafe-adjacent enthusiasts rather than mass retail
T1.first_claim: Prosumers pay a premium for commercial-grade components and brand credibility, so a Simonelli home line sold on that heritage (e.g., the Oscar Mood's commercial-derived parts) could earn premium prices without a new product category.

T2.claim: In prosumer espresso, value is captured by whoever controls consumer marketing and retail reach, not by the machine's commercial pedigree. Simonelli would earn more by partnering with or acquiring a consumer-channel player than by building its own home line.
T2.who_benefits: A consumer appliance group with retail and marketing reach (e.g., Breville, which bought Lelit), and a manufacturer like Simonelli that licenses or sells through them.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Home buyers choose by brand familiarity, retail availability and reviews; a professional pedigree does not reach them without consumer marketing and shelf presence.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Acquisition or licensing that gives access to an established consumer brand, distribution and marketing, with Simonelli supplying the engineering and components.
assumptions: Consumer appliance groups are willing to buy or license prosumer espresso brands at a premium
Consumer reach matters more than product pedigree for purchase decisions
Simonelli's professional business is not harmed by a consumer partner's brand
predictions: Acquisitions in prosumer espresso are driven by a buyer's distribution and marketing, not by production capacity
Brands with weak consumer reach but strong pedigree sell fewer units in retail tests than brands with strong marketing and similar specs
Simonelli would sell through partners rather than own a consumer brand, with deal value tied to channel access
T2.first_claim: In prosumer espresso, value is captured by whoever controls consumer marketing and retail reach, not by the machine's commercial pedigree. Simonelli would earn more by partnering with or acquiring a consumer-channel player than by building its own home line.

X1.name: Pedigree vs channel messaging price test for a home machine
X1.method: Online randomised test: a home-espresso product page (existing Oscar Mood or similar machine, no new hardware) shown to prospective home buyers. Three arms: (a) commercial-pedigree message at a 25% premium over a comparable mass-market home machine, (b) neutral message at the same premium, (c) same pedigree message delivered via a known consumer retailer's storefront. Measure pre-orders or add-to-cart at the displayed price. Ads bought on search and social targeting home-coffee interest.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 3,000 unique visitors per arm (about 9,000 total), recruited through paid search and social ads aimed at home espresso enthusiasts. Estimated, not observed.
X1.measure: Conversion to a refundable pre-order (or add-to-cart with email capture) per arm, with 95% confidence intervals, plus stated purchase reasons from a short exit survey.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm (a) converts clearly better than arm (b) at the same price, showing pedigree carries a premium. Arm (c) adds little beyond (a).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm (c) converts better than (a), because retailer presence and familiarity drive purchase; pedigree wording alone adds little over (b).

X1.decision_rule: Favour T1 if arm (a) conversion is at least 1.3 times arm (b) with non-overlapping 95% intervals, and arm (c) does not exceed arm (a) by more than 10%. Favour T2 if arm (c) is at least 1.3 times arm (a) with non-overlapping intervals. If neither holds, treat both as unsupported and do not commit capital to either line.

revisions.reason: SYN-SIMO-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not real data, so I do not cite it. It compares a home-barista skill lesson with a product-specification orientation. It does not test pedigree messaging against neutral messaging at a premium, so it neither supports nor weakens T1, and it changes nothing for T2. T1 stays open because the Oscar Mood source shows the commercial-component strategy exists, but it gives no price or sales data.

SYN-SIMO-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not real data, so I do not cite it. It tests a skill lesson against a product orientation, not consumer-channel reach against pedigree, so it does not bear on T2. T2 stays open: the Breville and Lelit source shows a consumer group bought a prosumer brand, but it does not show why.

What-if only: if SYN-SIMO-UPDATE were real, its lesson-versus-orientation contrast would bear on learning and hobby engagement, not on whether commercial pedigree earns a price premium. It would change nothing for T1. It is not evidence and will not be cited in finish.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a new consumer product line yet. Simonelli already sells a home-oriented machine (the Oscar Mood, built on commercial-derived components), so a pedigree-led home line is the more plausible next step. Before any investment, run the proposed pedigree-versus-channel price test (about 14,000 EUR and 8 weeks, both estimates) to decide between a pedigree-led home product and a channel partnership. If neither result clears the threshold, do not invest in either.
final.target_customer: Home espresso enthusiasts willing to pay a premium for commercial-grade equipment. This segment is inferred from the Oscar Mood and Victoria Arduino E1 Prima positioning and is not sized from data.
final.value_proposition: Commercial-grade components and professional heritage in a home machine, priced above mass-market home brands. Whether buyers pay that premium is the open question the test is designed to answer.
final.next_action: Design and run the price-and-messaging test (X1), with pre-order conversion across pedigree, neutral and retailer-storefront arms, and check the decision rule before launching. In parallel, look for Oscar Mood sales and margin data, which I could not find in public sources.
final.uncertainty: High. I found no public financial data on Simonelli's home or consumer lines: no sales, volumes, margins or price history for the Oscar Mood or E1 Prima. I found no independent evidence on whether buyers pay a premium for commercial pedigree. The sources I read were trade-press launch pieces and company product pages, so they show that the strategies exist, not that they pay. The Breville and Lelit source does not show why the acquisition happened. The one synthetic update was not used as evidence. Search coverage was limited to 8 searches, with 6 left unused.
would_change_if: The X1 test shows the pedigree arm converting at least 1.3 times the neutral arm at the same premium, with non-overlapping 95% intervals (supports T1)
The retailer-storefront arm converts at least 1.3 times the pedigree arm with non-overlapping intervals (supports T2 and a channel partnership)
Public or disclosed Oscar Mood sales or margin data show the home line is small or unprofitable, which would argue for no expansion
Evidence that consumer appliance groups buy prosumer brands for product rather than channel reasons would weaken T2
A concrete partner offer to license or distribute, which would make a channel route cheaper to test than building a line

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: SYN-SIMO-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not real data. Taken only as a what-if, it compares a home-barista skill lesson with a product-specification orientation, and the lesson arm has fewer reservations (32 against 72). It does not compare pedigree messaging with neutral messaging at a premium, so it neither supports nor weakens T1's claim that commercial heritage earns a price premium. It also rules out nothing in T2. It changes nothing, and I do not cite it as evidence.

In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
